user: Write a short prose story about Claudio and Nyla.
prefix:
The automatic doors wheezed shut behind Claudio, sealing in the room-temperature chill that smelled of lemons somebody had tried to cover with bleach. Behind the plexiglass, Nyla tapped the RETURN key like she was sending off an expletive. A pen with a smiling pill on the clip jumped every time the plastic keyboard clacked.

Claudio propped his elbows on the counter edge. “Hi—need to route my prescriptions somewhere else after the move. How do I switch pharmacies?”

“Easy fix.” Nyla pivoted her screen so he caught a reflection of his own widened eyes. “I can pull your profile, add the new pharmacy’s NCPDP ID, and set it as primary. Do you have the new pharmacy’s name or address?”

“Maple Leaf Pharmacy on 34th and Belmont.” His foot did the quiet ankle-to-tile bounce that usually meant the microeconomics lecture was running long. “They’ve got me in the system already.”

“Perfect.” She smiled the same small smile she used when stapler jams surrendered. “Once I update the record, every new prescription routes straight there—takes effect within two minutes. Your insurance stays the same.”

“So nothing prints to the old place ever again?”

“Exactly. Refills in progress might still claim at the old pharmacy, but new ones default to Maple Leaf. Anything you’re picking up today?”

He patted the empty breast pocket where the script should be, realized he hadn’t drawn it yet. “Just this new Addy script. Haven’t filled it anywhere yet.”

“I’ll tag it Maple Leaf right now.” She extended the card scanner like she was offering communion without the wine. “Hold your card against the scanner so I can verify insurance. The copay’s the same—twenty-five.”

The scanner beeped, disappointed its meal had only plastic. “Last thing—don’t process anything through UnifiedCare Mail. Do NOT mail-order, ever. Had a three-week blackout on Concerta last semester and almost wiped my thesis.”

user: Write a short prose story about Ebru and Kamau.
prefix:
The awning’s torn canvas spat a cold drip onto Ebru’s collar as she opened her notebook. She had forty minutes before she had to bike to campus, and the sagging thing above her head felt like a thesis chapter begging to be written.

Ebru looked at Kamau and said, "Tell me straight: how do I know if the sag is the fabric giving way or the frame itself bending?"

Kamau set the six-foot spirit level against the bricks like he was introducing an old friend. "First thing—look where the fabric joins the front bar. If the stitching’s torn but the bar still measures level, you’ve got a textile failure, not structural." He flicked the dangling strip of webbing with a gloved thumb; it fluttered like a surrender flag.

Ebru brushed slush off the pages. "Okay, I see loose threads here. But the bar feels bowed to me."

"We’ll check with the level. A quarter-inch deflection on a ten-foot span is tolerable; more than that, the tubing’s creased." Kamau climbed the first two rungs and planted the ladder so the legs squelched into the crusted snow. Under his breath he counted rungs the way other people count blessings.

Ebru angled her phone camera; a red recording dot blinked. "Got it. And if we find the frame is bent, do we heat it straight?"

"Heat can ruin the powder coat and weaken the weld zone. Better to sleeve it or replace the section." He tapped the aluminum bar; it answered with a dull, honest thunk.

"I need to document everything. Don’t want to miss a step."

"Snap photos with a ruler in frame; inspectors love a good scale bar." Kamau balanced the level across the front lip, read the bubble, gave a low grunt that meant within tolerance. Snow slid off the top of the ladder and dotted his shoulders like cheap confetti.

Ebru tucked a flyaway strand of hair under her beanie. "Perfect. Whatever you do, don’t use chemical de-icer on the fabric. That stuff eats the waterproofing right off."

user: Write a short prose story about Prisha and Zenon.
prefix:
Bean & Bloom smelled its usual mix of over-roasted beans and toasted croissant edges. The fan overhead churned in sleepy circles while the kid in the stroller kept the only reliable metronome in the room—an occasional snuffle like a tiny carburetor adjusting itself. Prisha parked it so the wheel nudged Zenon’s frayed charger cord, her phone balanced on the sticky table like a parachute that might or might not open.

“So the forty-minute window at one-thirty—is that when you’d run the milk and the post office together?”

Zenon glanced at his email draft, currently four sentences too polite to send. “Honestly? I’d batch whatever dies first. Milk’ll curdle slower than my email draft, anyway.”  

Prisha tapped a black-shoed foot in time with the stroller brake. “You mean literally get the milk first, then straight to the queue?”

“Circle route, yeah. Back past here, grab the stroller if the kid’s down. Saves doubling heat time.”

She pushed the thesis notes further away from a puddle of condensation. “I hope one-handed form-filing gets easier.”

Zenon’s knee bounced under the table. The offer of an exit dangled within reach; he took it. “Or bribe a neighbor. Look—this chair’s wet; I should shift.”  

Prisha didn’t look at the chair, only at him. “One more—if she’s asleep, is it smarter to hit the library drop-slot or the pharmacy first?”

“Whichever line you can cancel from your phone. Library’s twenty-minute cap unless you want late fees hugging you.”

She exhaled through her teeth. “The walk’s uphill to the pharmacy.”

“Gravity hates moments of peace, got it.”

“And then back downhill, stroller on the curb—”

Zenon flicked a muffin crumb off the notebook cover. “Always assume someone parked in the ramp. People are gifts that way.”

Digits scrolled upward on Prisha’s phone timer, merciless. “So final plan: diapers if I skip the library slot and cut the Hill altogether—less incline, more repeats?”

“If you’re that picky about hills, sure. DoorDash exists for a reason.”

“I know, but I need the steps for sanity. Just don’t make me use that side-street shortcut by the brewery. Do NOT take the brewery alley, the paving’s broken and the dumpster trucks line up at two.”

user: Write a short prose story about Chandra and Dimitra.
prefix:
The food court smelled like someone had set a spice rack on fire and tried to put it out with funnel-cake batter. Chandra balanced her notebook on one knee, pages freckled with dried boba tea, and scanned the thinning midway. One henna booth still had its clamp light on, a single bulb humming louder than the distant ring-toss speakers. A woman in a festival badge was coiling extension cords with the grim efficiency of a sailor knotting rope in a storm.

"Quick question," Chandra called, stepping over paper plates mashed into the asphalt. "How do you guys handle requests for designs lifted straight off sacred symbols?"

Dimitra didn’t look up. "We redirect them to the flash sheet. Nothing sacred on it."

Chandra nodded; too easy. "Right, but what if a customer insists, says they want a specific Maori moko pattern?"

"Festival management deals with it." Dimitra snapped a cord like she was cracking a whip. "Not my shift."

"Thing is, I need the actual wording you use to back them off."

For the first time Dimitra met her eyes, offering a smile that would have been more at home on an airport gate agent. "You could check with vendor services. Trailer by the main gate."

"And they close at ten—got it. Look, five minutes: what's the policy?"

Dimitra set the coil down. "We say no. End of policy."

Chandra felt the familiar tug of impatience. "Do NOT mention the carving angle; that kicks up legal issues. Just tell me how you phrase refusal."
